# Crossdating a Collection

:::{.callout-note title="Draft"}
First draft of the rewrite, 2026-10-22. The 2022 walk-through of `corr.series.seg`, `ccf.series.rwl` and the skeleton plots moves to [Fixing Errors](06FixingErrors.qmd). Every number in the text is computed when the book builds. Needs dev dplR 1.8.1 for the ring-edit methods that plant the errors and for `rwl.check` inside the report. Open questions are in the backlog.
:::

## Big Idea

Every ring in a collection is a claim about a year. For a living tree the outermost ring is the year you cored it, and every ring inside it is a count back from there. Miss one ring, a locally absent one or one too narrow to see, and every ring inside it is labeled a year too late. Count a false ring as real and every ring inside it is a year too early. [Chapter 2](02CoresToRecord.qmd) showed what that does to a chronology. Crossdating is the method you use to find dating errors.

Douglass did it by eye and with skeleton plots, and he was clear that no correlation formula should make a dating decision [@Douglass1941]. Richard Holmes's COFECHA added the statistics [@Holmes1983]. It cuts every series into overlapping segments, correlates each one with a master built from the other series, and flags the segments that fit badly or fit better somewhere else [@GrissinoMayer2001]. [Where dplR Comes From](01WhereDplRComesFrom.qmd) tells that story. For a generation of dendrochronologists COFECHA's output was what crossdating looked like on paper, and Grissino-Mayer's manual is how most of them learned to read it [@GrissinoMayer2001].

In `dplR` that job belongs to `xdate.report`. It builds a crossdating report in COFECHA's layout, because that layout is what people know how to read, and it tells you where it does things differently. In this chapter we break a collection we trust in two places and see whether the report finds both. Holmes was as clear as Douglass about what the statistics are for. They say where to look. The wood says what happened.

## Try It Interactively First

A confession before any code: for crossdating, a script is often the harder way to work. You look at a flag, try a shift, look at the core, insert a ring, and look again, and that loop is faster when you can click. That's what xDateR is for. It's a Shiny app that runs in a web browser, with nothing to install. It's built on `dplR`, `xdate.report` included, so its flags are the ones in this chapter. It has guided examples, and every report it writes includes R code that reproduces your edits from the original file. The [openDendro apps page](https://opendendro.org/apps/){target="_blank"} has the link to the live app, and the source is [on GitHub](https://github.com/OpenDendro/xDateR){target="_blank"}.

So why a chapter on doing it in code? Because the app is `dplR` underneath, and knowing what it is doing makes you better at using it. And because a script is a record. When a reviewer asks how you dated a collection, "I clicked around" is a worse answer than a file.

## Packages


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplR)
source("R/plant-dating-errors.R")
source("R/sim-collection.R")
```
:::




`R/plant-dating-errors.R` is a short script in the book's repository. It reads `co021` and misdates two of its series.

## Two Planted Errors

Mesa Verde is the right collection to break. Its series agree with each other about as well as any collection in the ITRDB, so any trouble the report finds is trouble we put there.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
co021Bad <- plant.dating.errors()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
35 series, 1176-1963, 0.01 mm.
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
planted <- attr(co021Bad, "planted")
planted
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  series year        error expected.lag
1 645221 1797 missing ring           -1
2 643143 1425   false ring            1
```


:::
:::




Series 645221 has lost its 1797 ring. The script deleted it with `delete.ring`, holding the outer ring at 1963, so every ring inside it slid a year later, and the series now starts in 1491 where it used to start in 1490. Series 643143 has its 1425 ring counted twice, and everything inside that slid a year earlier, to a start of 1226. Nothing else changed. These are the two mistakes a person makes counting rings, and [Fixing Errors](06FixingErrors.qmd) undoes them with the same two functions.

## The Report


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
co021Report <- xdate.report(co021Bad, title = "co021 with two planted errors")
```
:::


The whole report is a few hundred lines, in COFECHA's layout: a summary, the correlation of every segment of every series, a list of flagged segments, descriptive statistics for each series, the findings of `rwl.check`, and notes on how the report was made. `print(co021Report)` shows it all, and `write.xdate.report` saves it to a file, as plain text or as a web page. Here is the summary at the top.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# format() turns the report into lines of text. Lines 4 to 19 are the summary.
reportLines <- format(co021Report)
cat(reportLines[4:19], sep = "\n")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 Built with dplR's xdate.report(), not COFECHA; see the notes at the end.

      Measurement file name  : co021Bad
      Date checked           : 26OCT26
      Beginning year         : 1176
      Ending year            : 1963

      Series intercorrelation: 0.868
      Avg mean sensitivity   : 0.590
      Avg standard deviation : 0.315
      Avg autocorrelation    : 0.634
      Number dated series    : 35
      Segment length tested  : 50

      Number problem segments: 18  (A 0, B 18)
```


:::
:::




What did it do? Every series was divided by a 32-year spline and then prewhitened with an autoregressive model, which leaves the year-to-year wiggles and takes out each tree's slow trend and its memory. Each series was cut into 50-year segments that overlap by 25 years, and each segment was correlated with a master built from all the other series. Then each segment was slid up to 10 years either way to see whether it fit better somewhere else. Those are COFECHA's defaults. Why a spline, why 32 years, and why prewhiten at all is a story for the [aside on the crossdating statistics](07xAsideCrossdatingStats.qmd).

Of the 718 segments tested, 18 are flagged. COFECHA's two flags are kept as Grissino-Mayer describes them [@GrissinoMayer2001, p. 212]. An A flag is a segment whose correlation with the master is below the critical value, 0.3281 here, and that doesn't fit any better anywhere else. A B flag is a segment that correlates better with the master at some other position than where it is dated.

## Reading the Flags

A picture first. Each series is a bar, cut into its segments.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(co021Report$crs)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Segment correlations for `co021` with two planted errors. Blue segments correlate well with the master where they are dated, purple ones correlate better at another position (B flags), and red ones are weak but best where they are (A flags). Green marks the ends of a series where a full segment can't be tested.](05Crossdating_files/figure-html/xdate-crs-plot-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Two series have runs of purple, and nothing else does. The list of flagged segments says what each run means.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The flagged segments, with the correlations rounded to two places
flagShow <- flagged[, c("series", "from", "to", "flag", "r.dated", "best.lag", "r.lag")]
flagShow$r.dated <- round(flagShow$r.dated, 2)
flagShow$r.lag <- round(flagShow$r.lag, 2)
flagShow
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   series from   to flag r.dated best.lag r.lag
1  643143 1250 1299    B   -0.02        1  0.84
2  643143 1275 1324    B    0.17        1  0.94
3  643143 1300 1349    B    0.19        1  0.89
4  643143 1325 1374    B    0.18        1  0.84
5  643143 1350 1399    B    0.31        1  0.90
6  643143 1375 1424    B    0.17        1  0.91
7  643143 1400 1449    B    0.20        1  0.75
8  645221 1500 1549    B    0.20       -1  0.88
9  645221 1525 1574    B    0.06       -1  0.85
10 645221 1550 1599    B   -0.02       -1  0.89
11 645221 1575 1624    B   -0.06       -1  0.92
12 645221 1600 1649    B   -0.09       -1  0.95
13 645221 1625 1674    B   -0.18       -1  0.96
14 645221 1650 1699    B   -0.10       -1  0.93
15 645221 1675 1724    B   -0.03       -1  0.90
16 645221 1700 1749    B   -0.03       -1  0.90
17 645221 1725 1774    B   -0.04       -1  0.91
18 645221 1750 1799    B   -0.07       -1  0.92
```


:::
:::




Start with 645221. Every flagged segment, from 1500 to 1799, correlates with the master at about -0.04 where it is dated and at about 0.91 one year over. The sign of the lag says which way. `dplR` follows COFECHA here: a negative lag means the series lines up with the master when it is moved a year earlier, so its rings are dated too late, so a ring is missing. After the run, the segments are fine. The error is where the misdating stops, in the last flagged segment, 1750 to 1799. The ring we deleted was 1797.

Now 643143. Same pattern, opposite sign: lag 1 from 1250 to 1449, which means rings dated too early and a ring counted that isn't there. The last flagged segment is 1400 to 1449. The duplicated ring was 1425.

The report found both errors and flagged nothing else. In both series the planted year falls in the last flagged segment. That's as far as a report can take you: it gives you fifty years to search. [Fixing Errors](06FixingErrors.qmd) narrows that down with finer tools, and then with the core itself.

Notice how big the gains are, too. A dated correlation near zero becomes one near 0.9 with a one-year shift. Gains like that are what a dating error looks like in a collection this strong. A flag where the shift gains only a few hundredths may be noise, and the next section is about where those come from.

## Segments Find What a Whole Series Hides

The report ends with the findings of `rwl.check`, which checks each series as a whole against the master. Here is what that found.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The report keeps rwl.check()'s findings. Show the errors and warnings and
# leave out the notes.
checkFindings <- as.data.frame(co021Report$check)
checkFindings[checkFindings$severity != "note", c("check", "severity", "series", "value")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
               check severity series     value
1     RWL_DATING_LAG    error 645221 -1.000000
2 RWL_SERIES_OUTLIER  warning 645221  0.328438
```


:::
:::




It catches 645221 and misses 643143. Why? Only the first 199 of 643143's 738 rings are misdated, and averaged over the whole series the correctly dated part carries it: its correlation with the master is 0.70, lower than the collection's median of 0.89 but well clear of any alarm. 645221 is misdated over most of its length and falls to 0.33. That is the reason COFECHA cut series into segments in the first place. An error near the inner end of a long core barely moves a whole-series correlation, and a segment that contains it can't hide it.

## When the Signal Is Weak

Mesa Verde makes this look easy. Its series correlate with the master at 0.87 on average, and that is near the top of the ITRDB. Most collections are weaker, and a weaker collection can't find errors as reliably, and it raises flags on series that are dated correctly. How much weaker before the report stops being useful?

That's a question for a collection where we know the answer. The simulated stand from [Chapter 2](02CoresToRecord.qmd) has one missing ring, in SIM03A at 1800, and I can turn its common signal down. Here it is at three strengths, twenty simulated stands each. The code below handles one stand at a time in `weakRun`: build the stand, run `xdate.report` on it, and record whether SIM03A's missing ring was found and how many flags landed on series with nothing wrong. The loop runs it sixty times, and the last step averages each group of twenty.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# One simulated stand: build it, run the report on it, and count what the
# report got right and what it flagged that isn't wrong.
weakRun <- function(rbar, seed) {
  # cores from one tree always agree more than cores from different trees,
  # so rbar.wt moves up and down with rbar.bt
  sim <- sim.collection(rbar.bt = rbar, rbar.wt = rbar + 0.2, seed = seed)
  report <- suppressWarnings(xdate.report(sim$rwl))
  f <- report$flagged
  planted <- f$series == "SIM03A"   # the one series with a real error
  data.frame(
    rbar = rbar,
    # the correlation with the master that the report prints at the top
    corr = weighted.mean(report$stats$corr, report$stats$n.years,
                         na.rm = TRUE),
    # did SIM03A get a B flag at lag -1 that isn't "weak at every lag"?
    found = any(planted & f$flag == "B" & f$best.lag == -1 & !f$weak),
    # flags on series that have nothing wrong with them
    falseB = sum(!planted & f$flag == "B" & !f$weak),
    falseA = sum(!planted & f$flag == "A"),
    segments = sum(report$stats$n.seg)
  )
}

# Twenty stands at each of three signal strengths, one row per stand.
weak <- NULL
for (rbar in c(0.4, 0.2, 0.1)) {
  for (seed in 1:20) {
    weak <- rbind(weak, weakRun(rbar, seed))
  }
}

# Average the twenty stands at each strength, strongest first.
weakTable <- aggregate(cbind(corr, found, falseB, falseA, segments) ~ rbar,
                       data = weak, FUN = mean)
weakTable <- weakTable[order(-weakTable$rbar), ]
round(weakTable, 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  rbar corr found falseB falseA segments
3  0.4 0.60  1.00   1.15   1.15   257.35
2  0.2 0.41  0.85  16.40  26.75   257.25
1  0.1 0.28  0.45  32.65  46.80   257.45
```


:::
:::




`rbar` is the between-tree correlation I built in, `corr` the average correlation with the master that the report would print at the top, `found` the share of stands where SIM03A got a B flag at lag -1, and the last three columns the false flags and the number of segments tested, per stand. At the default strength the series correlate with the master at about 0.60, against 0.59 for Hurricane Ridge, and the missing ring is found every time, with about one false B flag per stand among 257 segments. Halve the shared signal and the master correlation drops to 0.41. The report still finds the missing ring in 85 percent of stands, and it now raises 16 B flags and 27 A flags on series that are dated correctly. At 0.28 it finds the error 45 percent of the time, under 33 false B flags and 47 false A flags per stand.

So read a report with the collection's strength in mind. In a collection like Mesa Verde a B flag is very likely a dating problem. In a weak one most B flags are noise, and the size of the gain is a better guide than the letter. The report helps: a B flag whose best correlation is itself below the critical value is marked "weak at every lag", and I left those out of the counts above. [Fixing Errors](06FixingErrors.qmd) is about what to do with a flag once you have one.

## Wrapping Up

`xdate.report` cuts every series into segments, correlates each against a master built from the rest, and flags the segments that fit badly or fit better a few years away. On a strong collection it found both planted errors, gave the direction of each, and put each within half a century. It didn't find the rings themselves, and it can't tell you what happened in the tree. A locally absent ring that nobody marked and a ring the measurer skipped look exactly the same to it. It found the two errors because Mesa Verde's trees agree so well, and on a weaker collection the same flags mean less.

The next chapter, [Fixing Errors](06FixingErrors.qmd), takes the two flagged series from half a century down to a year, puts the rings back, and runs the report again.

## Exercises

1. Plant your own error. Use `delete.ring` or `insert.ring` on a series of your choice in `co021`, near the inner end of a long series, and see whether `xdate.report` finds it. Does `rwl.check` on its own?
2. Run `xdate.report` on `co021Bad` with `seg.length = 30` and again with `seg.length = 100`. How do the runs of flags change, and what do you gain and lose with each?
3. Change `nyrs` to 20, the spline Holmes first used, and to 100. Do the same errors show up?
4. Run `xdate.report` on `wa082`, read from `data/wa082.rwl`. Which series does it flag, at what lags, with what gains? Which core would you pull out of the drawer first, and why? Nobody has planted anything here, and nobody knows the answer.
5. Open xDateR's example data in the app and find the errors planted there.

## Further Reading

- @Holmes1983 is COFECHA's first description. It is short, and it explains why the segments and the spline are there.
- @GrissinoMayer2001 is the COFECHA manual, with a tutorial on reading every part of the output. Most of what `xdate.report` prints is described there.
- @Douglass1941 is the founder of the field on what crossdating is and on why a correlation can't replace looking at the samples.
- @Bunn2010 describes `dplR`'s crossdating functions as they were first written. Some defaults have changed since. Please cite it if you use `dplR` for crossdating.
